StableHLO can be an exchange boundary between a framework and a compiler. A consumer that provides StableHLO-to-Linalg conversion may then bufferize and lower to affine loops or vectors.
XLA has its own HLO optimization and backend pipelines. It does not require the full route in this heading. Whether a TensorFlow program uses XLA also depends on how compilation was requested. XLA architecture.

TOSA-to-Linalg lowering translates supported tensor operations into structured computations. Tiling and vectorization can then prepare those computations for LLVM lowering. Layout changes, quantization, and operation coverage determine what extra work is needed. There is no single convolution rewrite that covers every type and target. TOSA dialect.
key optimization passes
tiling
Tiling splits an iteration space into bounded pieces so reused data may remain close to the computation. For an f32 matmul tile of sizes (M_t,N_t,K_t), the three dense operand tiles occupy
4\bigl(M_tK_t+K_tN_t+M_tN_t\bigr)\text{ bytes}.
With (256,256,128), that is 512\,\mathrm{KiB} before packing or other live data. Cache capacity, layout, concurrency, and the target’s instructions determine whether that tile fits and how efficiently it runs.
Tensor tiling also has a correctness obligation: each reduction tile must receive the preceding tile’s accumulator. The full result must be carried through the surrounding loops. Transform tutorial.
fusion
Producer-consumer fusion computes the part of a producer needed by a consumer tile. For a matmul followed by an elementwise operation, this can avoid writing and rereading the entire intermediate matrix. Other uses of that matrix may still require materialization or recomputation.

A bias or nonlinear activation must be applied at the correct point relative to the reduction. Adding the bias once per reduction tile changes the answer. Fusion needs both indexing information and the scalar computation’s semantics. Structured transformations.
vectorization
Vectorization groups scalar work into vector operations. For a simple contiguous loop, a width of eight processes eight elements per main-loop iteration. A length that is not divisible by eight needs masking, padding, or a remainder path.
For a contraction, the lowering also chooses how vectors map to registers and matrix instructions. Wider IR vectors can increase register pressure. Inspect the generated code and measure the actual kernel before treating vector width as a speedup. Vector dialect.
buffer allocation
The useful question is which old values remain observable after a proposed in-place update. If a later operation reads the original tensor, overwriting its only buffer would change that read. Bufferization must keep the old value available.
A destination passed through loop arguments can make storage reuse visible to analysis. An unrelated tensor.empty inside every iteration does not establish that one allocation will be hoisted and reused. Check the resulting memref IR, then account for ownership and deallocation. Bufferization analysis.
canonicalization and folding
Folding evaluates or simplifies an operation using its defined semantics. Canonicalization applies local cleanup patterns repeatedly, with limits. It is best-effort; a correct pipeline must not depend on every possible cleanup firing. CSE removes equivalent computations when the effect and dominance conditions permit it. Canonicalization.
Arithmetic identities need types and assumptions. Integer addition by zero is straightforward. Floating-point rewrites must respect signed zero, NaNs, rounding, and any fast-math permissions. A familiar algebraic identity is insufficient justification for changing an arith operation’s behavior.
loop transformations
Interchange changes loop order. For row-major storage, making the last index vary in the innermost loop gives contiguous accesses. Dependencies can forbid that order, so checking layout is only the performance half of the decision.

Skewing changes the coordinates of the iteration space; unroll-and-jam duplicates outer iterations and combines their inner loops. Each transformation must preserve dependencies, and floating-point reductions may impose additional ordering constraints. Affine dialect.
MLIR vs traditional compilers
vs LLVM
LLVM IR provides a defined instruction set for optimization and code generation. MLIR lets a compiler define operations that retain language or domain structure, then lower them when needed. The projects share infrastructure, and an MLIR compiler can use LLVM as its backend. MLIR’s representation.
vs XLA HLO
XLA is a compiler; HLO is one of its representations. StableHLO is an MLIR dialect used for exchange, with a compatibility contract. These names refer to different layers of a compiler stack. Asking whether a system uses “MLIR or StableHLO” misses that StableHLO is represented using MLIR. XLA architecture, StableHLO compatibility.
vs TVM
TVM provides a tensor compilation stack with graph-level and tensor-program representations, scheduling, and runtime components. Its architecture documentation describes Relax and TensorIR, so the older shorthand “Relay plus TIR” needs a version attached.
MLIR supplies reusable IR and transformation infrastructure. A project using it still has to choose its scheduling policy, runtime, and supported models. A count of IR levels tells us little about those decisions. TVM architecture.
reusability story
A transformation can work across operations that implement the contracts it needs. This is why Linalg exposes structured indexing and why dialects implement interfaces. Reuse stops where semantics or representations stop matching. Sharing the parser and pass manager alone cannot make an optimization valid for a new dialect. Linalg transformations.

TensorFlow ecosystem
TFRT uses MLIR to represent host programs and translates them to its Binary Executable Format for execution. That is a specific runtime design. Its repository documents the compiler-to-BEF path; it does not establish that TFRT replaced every TensorFlow execution path. TFRT.
IREE (Intermediate Representation Execution Environment)
IREE includes both an MLIR-based compiler and a runtime. Its compiler has input conversions, kernel code generation, and dialects for dispatch and execution, including Flow, Stream, HAL, and VM. The runtime supplies device interfaces and executes the compiled module.
Keeping host scheduling separate from kernel lowering matters: compiling an individual matmul does not determine when its buffers are available or when another device may use the result. IREE developer overview.
Torch-MLIR
Torch-MLIR bridges FX and ONNX entry points to MLIR-based compilers. Its import paths and conversions are useful to downstream projects such as IREE. Selecting Torch-MLIR means selecting an integration with a supported input subset and backend. The default torch.compile backend remains TorchInductor. Torch-MLIR, PyTorch torch.compile.
Flang (Fortran compiler)
Flang parses and checks Fortran before lowering into MLIR-based representations. HLFIR retains higher-level Fortran expression and assignment semantics; FIR represents lower-level Fortran operations and eventually lowers toward LLVM. Describing the entire frontend as MLIR would skip its parser and semantic analysis. Flang phases, HLFIR.
CIRCT (Circuit IR Compilers and Tools)
CIRCT uses MLIR for hardware compilation. Its dialects include HW for hardware structure, Comb for combinational logic, Seq for sequential logic, and SV for SystemVerilog constructs. Hardware descriptions are a useful counterexample to the claim that every MLIR pipeline ends in LLVM machine code. CIRCT documentation.

practical code examples
simple dialect definition
Start with the Toy tutorial for a buildable custom dialect. A constant operation needs an attribute whose type matches the result; an elementwise addition needs shape and element-type rules. A custom assembly format needs its parser and printer definitions too.
ODS can generate the structural code, while the dialect supplies semantics and lowerings. A bare declaration of toy.add does not make its arithmetic executable. For experiments with matmul, the existing arith, tensor, and linalg operations above already provide those definitions.
pattern rewriting example
Use a small integer fold to inspect the existing canonicalizer. Save this as fold.mlir:

func.func @fold() -> i32 {
  %a = arith.constant 7 : i32
  %b = arith.constant 9 : i32
  %sum = arith.addi %a, %b : i32
  return %sum : i32
}

mlir-opt fold.mlir --canonicalize
The result should return an i32 constant of 16; SSA names and printer formatting may change. This tests an existing folder without introducing a custom floating-point constant evaluator. Canonicalization and folding.
tiling transformation
This example tiles only the reduction dimension of a matmul. Keeping the output dimensions intact makes the loop-carried accumulator visible. The tile size divides the static reduction extent exactly.

func.func @matmul_buffer(%A: memref<8x16xf32>, %B: memref<16x8xf32>, %C: memref<8x8xf32>) {
  linalg.matmul ins(%A, %B : memref<8x16xf32>, memref<16x8xf32>)
                outs(%C : memref<8x8xf32>)
  return
}

mlir-opt matmul-buffer.mlir --convert-linalg-to-loops
The caller initializes %C and keeps its storage separate from %A and %B. The pass expresses the computation with SCF loops, loads, arithmetic, and stores. Tensor-form input needs bufferization or an appropriate tensor transformation first. Linalg loop lowering.
For a custom dialect conversion, declare which operations are legal in the result, provide rewrite patterns, and use a type converter where representations change. A full conversion fails if illegal operations remain. That failure is useful evidence of a missing lowering. Dialect conversion.

The manifold hypothesis says that a high-dimensional data distribution may concentrate near a set with much smaller intrinsic dimension. Exact support on one smooth manifold is an idealization. Measurement noise, discrete classes, and several data-generating processes can instead produce a neighborhood of several manifolds or a more general stratified set.
For an ambient space \mathbb R^D, the model assumes a d-dimensional manifold \mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^D with d\ll D. Local coordinates then need d variables to describe movement along \mathcal M, even though each observation still has D coordinates.
1310.0425⁠ (Fefferman et al., 2013)  make the claim testable by bounding four quantities: intrinsic dimension, volume, reach, and mean squared distance from the data distribution to a candidate manifold. Reach controls how sharply the manifold can bend or approach itself before nearest-point projection becomes ambiguous.
what the hypothesis buys
Low intrinsic dimension can reduce dependence on the ambient dimension. Learning can still be hard because sample requirements can grow with intrinsic dimension, curvature, volume, noise, and the smoothness of the target function over the support.
Interpolation also needs a boundary. Two points have a continuous on-manifold path only when they lie in the same path-connected component. A straight line in pixel space or latent space can leave the data support. Methods such as manifold mixup use interpolation as a training regularizer. That evidence is too narrow to explain deep-learning generalization in general.
The data-manifold hypothesis concerns the geometry of observations. Information geometry studies a parametric family of probability distributions. The two constructions can meet in a generative model. Each needs its own assumptions.
Fisher information

Definition 1. score and Fisher information 

For a smooth parametric family \{p_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^k\}, the score is s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x) and the Fisher information matrix is
\mathcal I(\theta)
=\mathbb E_{x\sim p_\theta}[s_\theta(x)s_\theta(x)^{\mathsf T}]
=-\mathbb E_{x\sim p_\theta}[\nabla_\theta^2\log p_\theta(x)],
where the second equality needs regularity conditions that permit differentiation under the integral and keep the support fixed.

Fisher information metric (Fisher-Rao)
When \mathcal I(\theta) is positive definite, it defines a Riemannian metric on the identifiable parameter space:
g_\theta(u,v) := u^{\mathsf T} \, \mathcal{I}(\theta) \, v \quad (u,v\in T_\theta\Theta\cong\mathbb{R}^k),
The local quadratic term of KL divergence is this metric:

1. KL local quadratic form 

For a small step \Delta\theta,
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{\theta} \Vert p_{\theta+\Delta\theta}\big)
= \tfrac{1}{2}\, \Delta\theta^{\mathsf T} \, \mathcal{I}(\theta) \, \Delta\theta
+ o(\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}).
Thus ds^2=d\theta^{\mathsf T}\mathcal I(\theta)d\theta measures local statistical distinguishability. See Kullback-Leibler divergence.


The uniqueness statement needs another assumption. Chentsov’s theorem characterizes the Fisher metric, up to scale, through invariance under sufficient statistics or the corresponding Markov morphisms. The KL expansion alone leaves the theorem unproved.
The eigenvalues of \mathcal I(\theta) measure local sensitivity to parameter perturbations. Riemannian curvature also depends on how the metric changes across the parameter space.
examples

Normal with known variance: x\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2I), parameter \mu\in\mathbb R^n.
\mathcal{I}(\mu) = \tfrac{1}{\sigma^{2}} I.
Poisson with rate \lambda: x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda).
\mathcal{I}(\lambda)=\tfrac{1}{\lambda}.
Normal with (\mu,\sigma) (single observation):
\mathcal{I}_{\mu\mu}=\tfrac{1}{\sigma^{2}},\qquad \mathcal{I}_{\sigma\sigma}=\tfrac{2}{\sigma^{2}},\qquad \mathcal{I}_{\mu\sigma}=0.

natural gradient
The natural gradient of an objective L(\theta) is
\tilde{\nabla} L(\theta) = \mathcal{I}(\theta)^{-1} \, \nabla L(\theta),
The steepest local descent direction under the Fisher metric is -\tilde{\nabla}L(\theta). This direction is invariant to smooth reparameterization in the continuous-time or infinitesimal-step description. A geodesic equation adds connection terms and specifies a path.
For a correctly specified likelihood model, the expected negative Hessian equals Fisher under regularity conditions. The observed Hessian can approach the same limit near a maximum-likelihood solution. Away from that setting, Fisher, the observed Hessian, and the 1905.12558⁠ (Kunstner et al., 2020)  are different matrices; see Maximum likelihood estimation.

empirical and expected Fisher 

The empirical Fisher \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i s_\theta(x_i)s_\theta(x_i)^{\mathsf T} replaces the model expectation with observed samples. It can give a poor curvature approximation away from a well-specified optimum. Diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations add another approximation for tractability.

empirical and expected Fisher 

The empirical Fisher \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i s_\theta(x_i)s_\theta(x_i)^{\mathsf T} replaces the model expectation with observed samples. It can give a poor curvature approximation away from a well-specified optimum. Diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations add another approximation for tractability.


pullback metrics on data/latent manifolds
Let a decoder g:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X map a latent coordinate z to an observation. The Jacobian J_g(z) pulls an observation-space metric back to the latent space. 1710.11379⁠ (Arvanitidis et al., 2021)  uses this construction to measure decoder distortion.
For the decoder model x\mid z\sim\mathcal N(g(z),\sigma^2I),
\mathcal{G}(z) = \tfrac{1}{\sigma^{2}} \, J_g(z)^{\mathsf T} J_g(z),
This metric measures how much a small latent displacement changes the decoder mean in observation space.
More generally, let a differentiable map \theta(z) choose the parameters of p_\theta(x). With J_\theta(z)=\partial\theta(z)/\partial z,
\mathcal G(z)=J_\theta(z)^{\mathsf T}\mathcal I(\theta(z))J_\theta(z).
Geodesics depend on the chosen metric. A shortest path under the decoder pullback can differ from a straight segment in latent coordinates. The path tests decoder distortion. A claim about data density needs a separate probability model; see geometric projections.
practical estimation

Estimate expected Fisher with samples from the model. The empirical Fisher uses the observed dataset, so it answers a different question.
For large models, diagonal, block-diagonal, and Kronecker-factored approximations trade accuracy for cost.
Decoder Jacobian singular values measure local stretching. Fisher eigenvalues measure local statistical sensitivity. Neither quantity alone is manifold curvature.

Summary 

Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter value that gives the observed sample the largest probability mass or density under a model. With independent data, maximizing likelihood is equivalent to minimizing negative log likelihood. Conditional classification likelihood gives the usual cross entropy objective.

definition
For a realized sample \mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n), the likelihood is the joint probability mass or density as a function of \theta:
\mathcal L(\theta;\mathbf x)=p_\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_n).
For independent and identically distributed observations,
\mathcal L_n(\theta;\mathbf x)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i),\qquad
\ell_n(\theta;\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(x_i).
The estimate for this sample is
\widehat\theta(\mathbf x)\in
\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell_n(\theta;\mathbf x)
=\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\bigl(-\ell_n(\theta;\mathbf x)\bigr).
When the sample \mathbf X is random, \widehat\theta_n(\mathbf X) is the estimator. This distinction matters in statements about bias and sampling distributions.
The score and observed information are
s_n(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\ell_n(\theta),\qquad
J_n(\theta)=-\nabla_\theta^2\ell_n(\theta).
For one observation, let s_\theta(X)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(X). The expected Fisher information is
\mathcal I_1(\theta)
=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[s_\theta(X)s_\theta(X)^{\mathsf T}\right]
=-\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\nabla_\theta^2\log p_\theta(X)\right],
where the second equality needs the usual differentiation and support conditions. For n i.i.d. observations, \mathcal I_n(\theta)=n\mathcal I_1(\theta).

Let \widehat p_n be the empirical distribution and q_\theta the model. The average negative log likelihood is exactly the empirical cross entropy:
-\frac{1}{n}\ell_n(\theta)
=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\log q_\theta(x_i)
=H(\widehat p_n,q_\theta).

connection to cross-entropy and KL
Let \widehat p_n be the empirical distribution and q_\theta the model. The average negative log likelihood is exactly the empirical cross entropy:
-\frac{1}{n}\ell_n(\theta)
=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\log q_\theta(x_i)
=H(\widehat p_n,q_\theta).
At the population level, for a true distribution p_0,
\mathbb E_{X\sim p_0}[-\log q_\theta(X)]
=H(p_0,q_\theta)
=H(p_0)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0\Vert q_\theta).
Because H(p_0) is independent of \theta, population maximum likelihood finds the model in the chosen class with the smallest forward KL divergence. The empirical objective estimates this population quantity.
training statistical models (derivation sketch)
For a joint model over observations z_i, the negative log likelihood is
\mathcal J_{\mathrm{joint}}(\theta)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(z_i).
For a discriminative classifier, inputs x_i are conditioned on rather than modeled:
\mathcal J_{\mathrm{cond}}(\theta)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i).
For one hard-label softmax example with logits a, the gradient is
\nabla_a\mathcal J=\operatorname{softmax}(a)-\operatorname{onehot}(y).
Mini-batch sampling gives an unbiased gradient estimate when the batch is sampled uniformly from the training set. See MLE derivation and gradients for the binary case.

penalty priors and MAP 

A prior adds its log density to the objective:
\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
\in\arg\max_\theta\{\ell_n(\theta)+\log p(\theta)\}.
A zero-mean Gaussian prior gives an L2 penalty. A Laplace prior gives an L1 penalty. 1711.05101⁠ (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) , as used by AdamW, is a different update rule, so the equivalence with an L2 objective usually fails. See regularization and MAP.


examples

Bernoulli( p)

Likelihood \mathcal L(p)=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n-\sum x_i} on p\in[0,1]. The estimate is \widehat p=\overline x, including the boundary cases where every observation is 0 or 1.



Poisson( \lambda)

For \lambda\geq0, \ell(\lambda)=\sum_i(x_i\log\lambda-\lambda-\log x_i!) and \widehat\lambda=\overline x.



Exponential( \lambda)

For \overline x>0, \ell(\lambda)=n\log\lambda-\lambda\sum_i x_i and \widehat\lambda=1/\overline x.



Normal( \mu,\sigma^2)

\ell(\mu,\sigma^2) = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (x_i-\mu)^2.
Solving gives \widehat\mu=\overline x and \widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2. The variance estimate is biased downward:
\mathbb E[\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2.
The usual unbiased sample variance multiplies it by n/(n-1).

properties (under regularity conditions)
For an identifiable, correctly specified model with an interior true parameter, enough differentiability, and nonsingular Fisher information,
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
\xrightarrow{d}
\mathcal N\!\left(0,\mathcal I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}\right).
The large-sample covariance of \widehat\theta_n is therefore approximately \mathcal I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}/n, or the inverse of the full observed information J_n(\widehat\theta) under the same conditions.
MLE is invariant under a one-to-one reparameterization: if \alpha=g(\theta), then \widehat\alpha=g(\widehat\theta). Under the stated conditions it is also asymptotically efficient.

caveats 


Under misspecification, MLE can converge to the KL projection within the model class. Its asymptotic covariance generally has the sandwich form rather than inverse Fisher.
Non-identifiability, boundary solutions, and singular Fisher information can break the normal approximation.
Finite-sample bias can remain, as in the Normal variance example.



practical notes

Optimize log likelihood rather than multiplying many small probabilities. Use log-sum-exp for softmax logits.
At a twice-differentiable interior local maximum, the Hessian of \ell_n is negative semidefinite. Negative definiteness is a sufficient local condition, not a necessary one.

A Merkle DAG is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are content-addressed. A node stores data and links to other nodes. Its hash covers both, so replacing a link changes the content being hashed. Several nodes can link to the same child, allowing them to share a subgraph.1
For a node v with data d_v and children c_1,\ldots,c_k, the construction is schematically
h_v = H\!\left(\operatorname{encode}(d_v,h_{c_1},\ldots,h_{c_k})\right).
The encoding fixes how the fields become bytes. We compute child identifiers before writing the nodes that reference them. In IPLD, links between blocks use CIDs, which include format information alongside the hash.2
Nodes are immutable: an update constructs new nodes. Consider a directory node linking to an essay and an image. Changing the essay creates a new essay node. A new directory node references that node and retains the existing image link. The old directory still describes the old contents while its blocks remain stored. Both versions share the unchanged image.
Given a trusted root identifier and the encoding rules, a reader can verify each fetched node and follow its verified links. This relies on the hash function resisting collisions and second-preimage attacks. Hashes establish byte identity, while storage and availability require a separate mechanism.

why cancellation works.
Each decrement step removes one occurrence of each of k distinct values: the k-1 tracked values and the arriving value. This is the cancellation argument in Misra’s proof.
Let D be the number of these steps and \widehat f(x) the counter at the end of the first pass, taking absent keys as zero. The removed groups contain kD occurrences, so
D \leq \left\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor.
A group removes at most one occurrence of any particular value. Therefore
f(x)-D \leq \widehat f(x) \leq f(x).
If f(x)>n/k, then \widehat f(x)>0, so every heavy hitter survives. A survivor can still fall below the threshold in the original input, which is why the exact recount matters.
example.
Take k=3 and b=(a,b,a,c,a,b,d,e). The map holds at most two keys.

After readingCountersa,b,a\{a:2,b:1\}c\{a:1\}a,b\{a:2,b:1\}d\{a:1\}e\{a:1,e:1\}
The arrivals c and d each cancel three distinct occurrences. The recount gives f(a)=3>8/3 and f(e)=1\leq 8/3, so the result is \{a\}. Both first-pass counters were 1; their equal residual counts concealed different frequencies.
cost.
With expected constant-time hash-map operations, both passes take expected O(n) total time and O(k) words of extra space. One decrement step touches k-1 counters. There are at most \lfloor n/k\rfloor such steps, so their total work is linear. This assumes keys and counters fit in machine words.
With a balanced search tree and constant-time key comparisons, the bound becomes O(n\log k) time. The original paper studies the comparison-based setting. The memory saving is useful when k is small relative to the number of distinct input values.

a sparse mixture-of-experts layer routes each token through a few feed-forward networks. a learned router selects the experts and weights their outputs. for token state x,
S(x)=\operatorname{TopK}(r(x),k),\qquad
y(x)=\sum_{e\in S(x)}g_e(x)E_e(x).
here r(x) contains routing scores, S(x) is the selected expert set, and g_e(x) weights expert E_e‘s output. gating and normalization vary by model. a shared expert, when present, runs for every token and adds another term.
with 64 equally sized routed experts and k=4, one token evaluates 4/64=1/16 of routed FFN work. the checkpoint still stores all 64 expert weight sets. attention, routing, shared experts, and cross-device communication add costs, so that fraction alone cannot predict memory use or latency. (Shazeer et al., 2017)
origins
the gated-expert idea dates at least to Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan, and Hinton’s 1991 paper, Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts. (Jacobs et al., 1991) Shazeer et al. developed the sparsely gated layer for large neural networks in 2017. Switch Transformer, first released in 2021, simplifies sparse routing to one selected expert per token. (Fedus et al., 2022; Shazeer et al., 2017)
routing also creates a training problem: repeatedly selecting the same experts concentrates both their updates and their workload. load-balancing mechanisms encourage broader use, while expert parallelism distributes weights and routes token states between devices.

definition
An NFA can have several next states for the same input symbol. It accepts a string when at least one path consumes the whole string and ends in an accepting state. A path that gets stuck rejects only that path.
I use a set of start states here:
\begin{aligned}
M &= (Q, \Sigma, \Delta, S, F) \\
\Delta &: Q \times \Sigma \to \mathcal{P}(Q) \\
S &\subseteq Q, \qquad F \subseteq Q.
\end{aligned}
Q is a finite set of states, \Sigma a finite alphabet, and \mathcal{P}(Q) the set of subsets of Q. The set \Sigma^* contains every finite string over \Sigma, including the empty string \epsilon. An omitted transition means \Delta(q,a)=\varnothing.
Let R_w be the states reachable after reading w. For an NFA without epsilon transitions:
\begin{aligned}
R_\epsilon &= S, \\
R_{wa} &= \bigcup_{q \in R_w} \Delta(q,a), \\
\mathcal{L}(M) &= \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid R_w \cap F \neq \varnothing\}.
\end{aligned}
This gives a direct simulation: keep the reachable states and update them for each symbol. Acceptance is checked after the last symbol. See Cornell’s NFA notes.

epsilon transition
An \epsilon-transition changes state without consuming a symbol. Extend the transition function to
\Delta:Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\epsilon\})\to\mathcal{P}(Q).
For A\subseteq Q, its epsilon closure E(A) contains every state reachable from A by zero or more epsilon transitions, including the states in A themselves. Simulation starts with R_\epsilon=E(S) and takes epsilon closure again after each consumed symbol. See Aho’s definition and construction.

Here S=\{s_1\}, F=\{s_4\}, and \Sigma=\{0,1\}. The language is
\mathcal{L}(M)=\{0^n1^m\mid n,m\in\mathbb{N}_0,\ m=0\text{ or }m\geq2\}.
The path through s_1 accepts any number of zeros, including none. Reading one 1 reaches s_2, which cannot accept. A second 1 reaches s_3; further ones stay there. No zero can follow a one. For example, \epsilon, 000, and 00111 are accepted; 1, 001, and 110 are rejected.
subset construction
A DFA can store the NFA’s entire reachable-state set as one state. For the epsilon convention above, construct
\begin{aligned}
Q_D &= \mathcal{P}(Q), \\
s_D &= E(S), \\
\delta_D(A,a) &= E\left(\bigcup_{q\in A}\Delta(q,a)\right), \\
F_D &= \{A\subseteq Q\mid A\cap F\neq\varnothing\}.
\end{aligned}
Starting from E(S), generate transitions until no new subsets appear. Only reachable subsets need to be stored. The empty subset is a rejecting sink: it maps to itself on every symbol. Without epsilon transitions, E(A)=A.

TCP carries a byte stream. A write() call adds bytes to that stream; its boundary need not survive as a packet boundary. Small segments have a cost: Nagle’s original example puts one byte of data behind forty bytes of TCP/IPv4 headers, a payload fraction of 1/41 before link-layer overhead. RFC 896 describes the resulting small-packet problem.
Nagle’s algorithm and Delay ACK
Nagle coalesces small writes while earlier data remains unacknowledged. With nothing outstanding, it permits a short segment. Otherwise, it holds new bytes until the outstanding data is acknowledged or enough bytes can be sent to fill a segment. MSS is the maximum TCP payload size, excluding headers. Congestion control and the receiver’s available window still constrain transmission. This is a send-policy rule, not a fixed batching timer. RFC 9293, §3.7.4
Delayed ACK is a receiver policy that reduces acknowledgement traffic. Consider a request split across two small writes: the first segment arrives, Nagle holds the second, and the receiver delays its ACK. The receiving application needs both parts before it can reply. Progress waits for the ACK timer. Exact behaviour depends on the TCP implementation and connection state.
Silly-window avoidance concerns small increments in the advertised receive window. It has separate sender and receiver rules; delayed ACK determines when an acknowledgement is sent. RFC 9293, §3.8.6
CORK algorithm
Linux’s TCP_CORK lets the application hold a partial segment while assembling output. For example, set it before writing a response header, add the file body with sendfile(), then clear it to release the remaining bytes. Full segments can leave while the socket is corked. The documented Linux timeout ceiling is 200\,\mathrm{ms}; clear the option when the output is ready rather than relying on that fallback.
TCP_NODELAY disables Nagle for latency-sensitive small writes. Other send constraints still apply. Linux lets TCP_CORK override it, although setting TCP_NODELAY explicitly flushes pending output even while corked. TCP_CORK is Linux-specific. tcp(7)

steady stokes: find (\mathbf{u},p) with -\nu\,\Delta\mathbf{u}+\nabla p=\mathbf{f}, \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}=0. on \mathcal{v}, the bilinear form a(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\nu\int \nabla\mathbf{u}:\nabla\mathbf{v} is continuous and coercive; lax–milgram yields a unique \mathbf{u}, and de rham’s theorem recovers p up to a constant.
oseen linearization: with a given \mathbf{w}, solve -\nu\,\Delta\mathbf{u}+ (\mathbf{w}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u}+\nabla p=\mathbf{f} via fixed-point/picard iteration on the variational problem; small data or large viscosity ensure convergence. this is the backbone of many fem/dg solvers.

recent research (weak solutions)

convex-integration constructions show nonuniqueness of finite-energy weak solutions in periodic settings and related frameworks (Buckmaster & Vicol, 2018).
non-uniqueness of leray solutions in the forced case (even with zero initial data) established by albritton–brué–colombo (Albritton et al., 2021).
quantitative advances on partial regularity and epsilon-regularity sharpen caffarelli–kohn–nirenberg-type results, informing weak–strong criteria (Lei & Ren, 2022).
preprint progress on nonuniqueness in \mathbb{r}^3 indicates further extensions beyond periodic domains (Miao et al., 2024).

Nesterov momentum evaluates the gradient where the accumulated momentum would take the parameters. This lets the gradient correction respond to that proposed move.1
idea:

extrapolate the current parameters using the previous displacement;
compute the gradient at this lookahead position;
take a gradient step from there.


definition 

Let f be the objective, \alpha>0 the step size, and \beta_t the momentum coefficient. Initialize v_0=0. Here v_t is a parameter displacement, including its sign and step-size scaling:
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \theta_t + \beta_t v_t, \\
v_{t+1} &= \beta_t v_t - \alpha\nabla f(y_t), \\
\theta_{t+1} &= \theta_t + v_{t+1}
                 = y_t - \alpha\nabla f(y_t).
\end{aligned}


Thus v_t=\theta_t-\theta_{t-1} after the first step. With a fixed step size, a gradient buffer b_t=-v_t/\alpha gives the equivalent convention
b_{t+1}=\beta_t b_t+\nabla f(\theta_t-\alpha\beta_t b_t),
\qquad
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\alpha b_{t+1}.
The lookahead sign and the factor \alpha depend on which quantity the buffer stores.
For a small example, take f(\theta)=\theta^2/2, \theta_t=1, v_t=-2, \beta_t=0.9, and \alpha=0.1. Momentum alone proposes y_t=-0.8, across the minimum at zero. The gradient there is -0.8, so the correction adds 0.08 and gives \theta_{t+1}=-0.72. Classical momentum would use the gradient at \theta_t=1 and reach -0.9. The lookahead changes the correction before the update is committed.
The usual convergence statements concern the objective gap f(\theta_T)-f(\theta^\star), with exact gradients, an attained minimum, and an L-Lipschitz gradient on \mathbb{R}^d. Convexity is essential to the following guarantees.2

Here D=\lVert\theta_0-\theta^\star\rVert_2, \Delta_0=f(\theta_0)-f(\theta^\star), and \kappa=L/m for m>0. These are upper bounds; an individual problem may converge faster.

1. parameters for strongly convex objectives 

For the strongly convex row, one standard accelerated choice is
\alpha=\frac{1}{L},
\qquad
\beta_t=\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}.
With v_0=0, it gives the finite bound
f(\theta_T)-f(\theta^\star)
\le \left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\right)^T
\left(\Delta_0+\frac{m}{2}D^2\right).


For a positive-definite quadratic with Hessian H, we can take L=\lambda_{\max}(H) and m=\lambda_{\min}(H). General functions need bounds valid across the domain. The smooth convex row uses a different, time-varying momentum schedule; plugging m=0 into the strongly convex formula does not supply it. Mini-batch noise and nonconvex neural-network losses also require their own analysis.

1844-1900
Reading notes on Twilight of the Idols (1889), with related passages from The Gay Science, Thus Spoke Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil.
Problem of Socrates.

Maybe something wrong with this? What drives Socrates from this demands with reasons and knowledge? What are the motives?

The question is about the need for rational control. Nietzsche reads the Socratic formula as \text{reason} = \text{virtue} = \text{happiness}. He treats this as a response to conflicting instincts: reason becomes their ruler because they can no longer govern themselves. His term decadence names that disorder and the remedies it demands. This is Nietzsche’s interpretation of Socrates, rather than an established account of his psychology. (Twilight, “The Problem of Socrates,” §§4, 9-11.)
The lecture formulation “An unexamined life is not worth living. Only Knowledge alone makes life worth living” joins Socrates’ claim about examination to a stronger claim about knowledge. The first has its source in Plato’s Apology 38a; the second needs an argument. Nietzsche’s challenge is to ask what kind of life needs that promise.
The same question applies to Plato‘s preference for stable being over becoming. Nietzsche asks what motivates a philosopher to treat change and the body as obstacles to truth. A motive can explain a commitment while leaving its truth unsettled. Discovering a need for reassurance would not, on its own, refute an argument.
In “The Problem of Socrates,” §2, Nietzsche argues that the value of life as a whole cannot be estimated.
Nietzsche’s reason is that a living judge is already a participant in life, while the dead cannot judge. A verdict on life as a whole therefore lacks the disinterested standpoint it claims. This leaves room to judge particular lives, commitments and acts. Life is still unfolding; a global verdict pretends to have finished it.
God is Dead
Nietzsche asks what happens to the commitments built around belief in God.
In The Gay Science §125, the madman announces God’s death to people who already disbelieve in God. Their disbelief has arrived before an understanding of its consequences. Section 343 identifies the event as the loss of credibility of the Christian God and asks what happens to the European morality supported by that belief. It also describes the prospect of new inquiry with excitement.
The further question in §344 concerns the unconditional value of truth. Scientific inquiry tests its claims, yet the decision to pursue truth at any cost is itself a commitment. Nietzsche asks whether that commitment retains the older faith that truth is divine. This challenges an inherited justification for valuing truth; it does not announce that scientific results have stopped being reliable.

Nihilism: the loss of authority of the values by which a life was directed. The problem remains after an argument against God’s existence succeeds: which commitments survive, and what supports them?
How do we have a duty to truth? Does atheism settle that question, or leave it open?
From Thus Spoke Zarathustra
In “The Tree on the Mountainside” (also translated “The Tree on the Hill”), Zarathustra distinguishes the noble person’s wish to create from the good person’s wish to preserve what already exists. The youth’s danger is becoming a bitter mocker who has given up that wish to create. The warning against becoming “a churl” in the lecture reader belongs to this passage. Mere opposition to accepted goodness supplies no new aim.
Morality as Anti-Nature
The target of this Twilight chapter is a treatment of passion: trying to remove desire because it can lead to harm. Nietzsche contrasts this with giving a passion a more developed form, as sensuality can become love and hostility can become a productive relation to an opponent. His claim concerns how desires are cultivated. It offers no guarantee that following a desire will be good. (§§1-3.)
The lecture phrase “Obstacles that are good for us: Becomes who we are” belongs with this question. Some resistance can develop a capacity; whether a particular obstacle does so needs to be shown. Calling suffering necessary for growth would leave that distinction out.
Nietzsche’s criticism of equality and democracy is related, with its own argument. He thinks an ideal centred on shared security and comfort can suppress the development of exceptional people. The “herd” names a pattern of shared valuation and pressure to conform. It is a polemical description of a kind of society, rather than a definition of every human association. (Beyond Good and Evil, §§44, 202.)
The worry behind my singularity shorthand is a single moral standard imposed on people with different capacities and aims. Nietzsche’s response is hierarchical: he denies that one morality benefits everyone equally. That judgment needs defending. Difference alone cannot establish which differences deserve authority.

John Stuart Mill is also a target, named among Nietzsche’s adversaries in “Skirmishes of an Untimely Man,” §1. Beyond Good and Evil §228 attacks English utilitarianism for treating its own conception of welfare as a universal goal. Mill’s defence of individuality gives them a point of contact; their standards for evaluating a life remain different. Nietzsche’s objections extend beyond Kantian duty.
“Morals compromise creativity” is the lecture summary. The useful question is which moral demand blocks which activity, and why that activity should take priority. Reversing every accepted judgment would leave the argument unfinished.
What I Owe the Ancients
This heading names a chapter of Twilight of the Idols. The Birth of Tragedy (1872) is an earlier work that the chapter revisits.
Greek tragedies in the lecture:

Aeschylus, Oresteia
Sophocles, Oedipus the King
Euripides, Bacchae


Why do we enjoy tragedies? Why do we enjoy watching people suffer?


“All becoming and growing - all that guarantees a future - involves pain.” (282)

Nietzsche connects this claim to procreation and the Dionysian mysteries in “What I Owe the Ancients,” §4. In §5, tragic affirmation means being able to affirm existence while confronting destruction and suffering. Enjoying a tragedy need not amount to wanting the depicted suffering to happen. Neither does this account show that every actual injury benefits its victim.

“Art is worth more than truth.”

This belongs with Nietzsche’s later reflections on The Birth of Tragedy, collected after his death in The Will to Power, §853 IV. That compilation is an editorial arrangement of notebooks, rather than a book he completed. The comparison concerns art’s power to sustain an affirmation of existence.
The lecture’s final contrast is that science supplies no purpose in itself, while art can create values. Knowing how something happens leaves open what to make of it. The further question is how a created value earns commitment. Incompleteness of our experience leaves that question open; it does not establish that life has no value.

The optimization theorem compares black-box search algorithms under a particular distribution of problems: every possible cost function is equally likely. Under this average, every non-revisiting algorithm produces the same distribution of observed costs. (Wolpert & Macready, 1997)

Theorem 1. 

Let X be a finite nonempty search space, Y a finite nonempty set of cost values, and \mathcal{F}=Y^X the set of all functions f:X\to Y. Each algorithm chooses an unvisited point using its previous observations, with optional internal randomness. For any two such algorithms a_1,a_2, any 1\leq m\leq |X|, and any cost sequence d_m^y\in Y^m,
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}} P(d_m^y\mid f,m,a_1)
=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}} P(d_m^y\mid f,m,a_2).
Here d_m^y=(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_m)) records the costs in query order. The inputs are distinct; their costs may repeat. The probability is over the algorithm’s randomness for a fixed function. The sum then averages over functions.


Assigning a uniformly random function amounts to choosing each input’s cost independently and uniformly from Y. Previous queries therefore give no information about any unvisited point. Adaptively choosing the next point cannot change its cost distribution.
For example, take X=\{1,2,3\} and Y=\{0,1\}. There are 2^3=8 functions. After two distinct queries, every search strategy has probability 1/4 of seeing each sequence (0,0), (0,1), (1,0) or (1,1). The expected minimum observed cost is consequently 1/4.
For a one-query comparison, average uniformly over the four nondecreasing functions instead. Querying the left endpoint then has expected observed cost 1/4; querying the right endpoint has expected observed cost 3/4. The structure changes which query is useful.

covers performance measures derived from the observed cost sequence, such as the best cost found after m distinct evaluations.

Described a situation, idea, or societal condition that George Orwell identified as being destructive to the welfare of a free and open society.

The Overton window describes the range of policies politicians can support without losing too much public backing. Joseph Overton developed the model at the Mackinac Center. Its boundaries depend on the society and the time.
A proposal outside the window can still be discussed, researched or defended. The constraint is the political cost of endorsing it. Public acceptance also says nothing by itself about whether a policy is sound.
The window can shift, widen or narrow as public beliefs and norms change. Advocacy and institutions can contribute to that change; merely stating an extreme position gives no assurance that support will follow.
Applying the term to general idea perception extends the model beyond its original policy setting. That use needs a specified audience: acceptable to whom, and with what consequence for dissent?

Definition 1. Arithmetic Intensity 

For operation \mathcal{O}:
\text{AI}(\mathcal{O}) = \frac{\text{FLOPs}(\mathcal{O})}{\text{Bytes}(\mathcal{O})}

\text{Arithmetic Intensity} = \frac{\text{Computation FLOPs}}{\text{Communication Bytes}}

\text{MI} = \frac{C}{\beta}

kv transport budget
transfer time per request is approximately
T_{\text{xfer}} \approx \frac{\text{kv\_bytes}}{\beta_{\text{net}}}\qquad \qquad \tag{4}
where \beta_{\text{net}} is end‑to‑end bandwidth between prefill and decode workers. for dp across racks, ensure \beta_{\text{net}} is high enough so T_{\text{xfer}} doesn’t dominate ttft; mla (eq. 2) can cut transfer volume 5–10×.
compatibility and layout

model identity: same weights, tokenizer, positional encoding (rope/yaRN), and attention variant on both tiers.
kv layout: match paged size and dtype; for gqa, kv heads are fewer than query heads. mla stores latents instead of per‑head kv.
moe: decode tier usually runs ep>1; prefill can use smaller ep or dense layers depending on router characteristics. keep connector aware of all‑to‑all intervals to avoid congestion.

scheduling and flow control

admission control: cap in‑flight prefills to avoid decode starvation.
backpressure: block or shed on lookupbuffer when decode lags.
placement: co‑locate prefill and decode within rack or on nvlink islands when using P2pNcclConnector.

failure modes

version skew: kv produced by model A@sha1 must not be consumed by A@sha2.
partial kv: ensure atomicity on insert; consumers should never see partial blocks (vLLM’s lookupbuffer insert/drop_select semantics). (vLLM Team, 2025)
retries: on connector failure, either re‑run tail‑prefill on decode or replay prefill after backoff.

PJRT gives ML frameworks a common interface to a hardware backend’s compiler and runtime. A framework uses it to discover devices, prepare input buffers, compile a computation, and execute it. Hardware providers implement the interface for targets such as TPUs and GPUs. The framework can call those implementations without knowing their internals. Google’s introduction describes this plugin boundary; the source contains the interfaces and implementations.
where compilation happens
StableHLO represents a computation as tensor operations. XLA optimizes that representation and generates code for a target. PTX is NVIDIA’s virtual instruction set, which a GPU compiler can emit on the way to native instructions. XLA architecture describes that compilation path.
PJRT defines how the framework requests compilation and uses the resulting executable. The plugin supplies the compiler and runtime behind those calls, so it can use XLA or another toolchain.
objects the framework handles
The C++ API overview names the main objects:

A client holds the state for communication with a backend and owns its devices and memory spaces.
A device identifies an execution target. Its memory spaces describe where data can live and which devices can access it.
A buffer holds input or output data in a memory space. Its ownership and readiness rules determine when data can be read, reused, or released.
A loaded executable holds a compiled computation ready to accept input buffers and produce output buffers.

following one computation
For a computation such as f(x) = x + 1, the framework first lowers the function to a program the backend accepts, such as a StableHLO module. Through PJRT_Client_Compile, it passes the program and compilation options to the backend and receives a loaded executable.
The framework prepares the input with PJRT_Client_BufferFromHostBuffer, then supplies the resulting buffer to PJRT_LoadedExecutable_Execute. The output buffer may be returned while the device is still working. PJRT_Buffer_ReadyEvent reports when the data is ready or an error has occurred; PJRT_Buffer_ToHostBuffer requests a transfer back to host memory. These operations and their ownership rules are specified in the C API header.
A hardware plugin exposes those C functions through a PJRT_Api function-pointer table in a shared library. Its implementation can use the C API directly or wrap PJRT’s C++ classes. That lets a framework load a backend without linking against its private C++ types. The integration guide covers both routes.

PageRank computes page scores from a link graph. Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd describe it in a Stanford report (Page et al., 1999); the draft is dated January 29, 1998. The score does not depend on the query, so a search engine computes it once per crawl and uses it for every query. This garden computes the same score over its own notes on pagerank.
From citations to links
Citation analysis counts how often other papers cite a paper. The report treats a link as a citation, so a page with many backlinks (inbound links) is probably important. Raw backlink counts fail on the web for two reasons. A web page costs nothing to publish, so anyone can make many pages that link to one target. And one link from the Yahoo home page says more about a page than many links from pages that nobody reads.
PageRank uses a recursive rule instead: a page has a high rank when the ranks of the pages that link to it add up to a large number. Many backlinks raise a page, and so do a few backlinks from high-ranked pages. A link contributes according to the source page’s rank and outgoing links, so counting backlinks alone misses part of the calculation.
The simplified rank
Let B_u be the set of pages that link to page u, and let N_v be the number of links on page v. The report first defines
R(u) = c \sum_{v \in B_u} \frac{R(v)}{N_v}
Each page divides its rank equally among its links, and each page receives the sum of the parts that arrive. The constant c keeps the total rank fixed.
The report’s Figure 3 is a small example. A links to B and C, B links to C, and C links to A. The ranks R(A) = 0.4, R(B) = 0.2, R(C) = 0.4 are a fixed point: A sends 0.2 on each of its two links, C receives 0.2 from A and 0.2 from B, and C sends all of its 0.4 to A.

The report’s Figure 3 is a small example. A links to B and C, B links to C, and C links to A. The ranks R(A) = 0.4, R(B) = 0.2, R(C) = 0.4 are a fixed point: A sends 0.2 on each of its two links, C receives 0.2 from A and 0.2 from B, and C sends all of its 0.4 to A.
In matrix form, let M_{uv} = 1/N_v when v links to u, and 0 otherwise. Then R = cMR, so R is an eigenvector of M.1 If every page has an outgoing link, each column sums to 1 and c = 1. Power iteration repeatedly multiplies an initial probability vector by M. It converges to a unique stationary distribution when the finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic. A two-page cycle already breaks convergence: all the mass alternates between the pages if it starts on one of them. Separate closed components can also give several stationary distributions.
Rank sinks and the random surfer
The simplified rule fails on closed loops. Take two pages that link only to each other, and a third page that links to one of them. Rank flows into the pair on every iteration and never leaves. The report calls this a rank sink.
The fix is a rank source E, a vector over pages:
R'(u) = c \sum_{v \in B_u} \frac{R'(v)}{N_v} + c\,E(u), \qquad \lVert R' \rVert_1 = 1
The report explains E with a random surfer who sometimes stops following links and starts elsewhere. Its experiments mostly used a uniform source with \lVert E \rVert_1 = 0.15. That source includes both a distribution over destinations and an amount of rank to inject.
To separate them, write E = e v, where e = \lVert E \rVert_1 and v is a probability vector. On a graph where every page has an outgoing link, summing the fixed-point equation gives
1 = c(1+e), \qquad c = \frac{1}{1+e}.

To separate them, write E = e v, where e = \lVert E \rVert_1 and v is a probability vector. On a graph where every page has an outgoing link, summing the fixed-point equation gives
1 = c(1+e), \qquad c = \frac{1}{1+e}.
The resulting equation is R' = cMR' + (1-c)v. Thus the report’s e = 0.15 gives c = 1/1.15 \approx 0.8696, rather than 0.85. A source of mass e = (1-d)/d gives a chosen damping factor d. This conversion assumes a column-stochastic link matrix; dangling pages need the treatment below.
The usual probability-normalized form instead chooses d = 0.85 directly. At each step the surfer follows a random link with probability d and restarts from v with probability 1-d. For uniform v, with N pages and L(q) links on page q:
\mathrm{PR}(p) = \frac{1-d}{N} + d \sum_{q \to p} \frac{\mathrm{PR}(q)}{L(q)}
\mathrm{PR}(p) is the long-run fraction of steps that the surfer spends on p.2 Without the jump, a surfer in a rank sink stays there. At d = 0.85, the mean wait until a restart is 1/(1-d) \approx 6.7 steps. A restart can land in the same sink. For a closed set of s pages under uniform restart, the mean wait to leave is 1/[(1-d)(1-s/N)] when s < N.
Dangling pages
A page with no links is dangling. Its rank flows nowhere, so the total rank shrinks on every iteration. In 1998 most dangling pages were pages that the crawler had not fetched yet: the 24 million downloaded pages pointed to 51 million URLs that were not downloaded. The report removes dangling pages, computes the ranks of the others, adds the dangling pages back, and iterates a few more times.

Dangling pages
A page with no links is dangling. Its rank flows nowhere, so the total rank shrinks on every iteration. In 1998 most dangling pages were pages that the crawler had not fetched yet: the 24 million downloaded pages pointed to 51 million URLs that were not downloaded. The report removes dangling pages, computes the ranks of the others, adds the dangling pages back, and iterates a few more times.
The usual choice now, and the one this garden makes, keeps dangling pages and treats each one as a link to every page. The surfer on a dangling page jumps at random:
\mathrm{PR}(p) = \frac{1-d}{N} + \frac{d}{N}\sum_{L(q)=0}\mathrm{PR}(q) + d \sum_{q \to p} \frac{\mathrm{PR}(q)}{L(q)}
With this term the scores always sum to 1, and no rank is lost.
Computing it
The report’s §2.6 prints the following lost-mass loop:
\begin{aligned}
R_{i+1} &\leftarrow A R_i \\
\delta_{\text{lost}} &\leftarrow \lVert R_i \rVert_1 - \lVert R_{i+1} \rVert_1 \\
R_{i+1} &\leftarrow R_{i+1} + \delta_{\text{lost}}\, E \\
\delta &\leftarrow \lVert R_{i+1} - R_i \rVert_1
\end{aligned}
It repeats until \delta < \epsilon. The final addition preserves total mass only if the E used in this loop sums to 1: multiplying the lost mass by a source of mass 0.15 replaces only 15\% of it. An undamped stochastic A loses no mass at all, so that reading of the loop also supplies no restarts. The report’s displayed source equation and loop therefore need their normalization conventions made explicit before use. Write \Delta_k=\lVert r_k-r_{k-1}\rVert_1. Since \Delta_1\le2, the bound is \Delta_k\le2d^{k-1}. With d = 0.85, a sufficient number of updates for \Delta_k\le10^{-10} is

Personalized PageRank
E decides which pages get rank without any links. A uniform E values every page simply because it exists. The report found one problem with it: groups of pages with many links among themselves, such as copyright notices, disclaimers and heavily interlinked mailing-list archives, get too much rank.
The other extreme puts all of E on one page. The report tried the Netscape home page and the home page of John McCarthy. In both cases that page ranked first, followed by the pages that it links to. Under McCarthy’s E, pages about computer science and Stanford ranked higher. The home page of John Mitchell, in the Stanford theory group, was at the 100.00 percentile under McCarthy’s view and at the 93.89 percentile under Netscape’s. To test PageRank for search, the authors built a search engine over the titles of 16 million pages. It finds every page whose title contains all the query words and sorts them by PageRank. A query for “university” returned a list of major universities, while AltaVista returned pages that looked random. PageRank helps most with underspecified queries: for “Stanford University” it puts the university home page first, above the many pages that mention Stanford. Google combines PageRank with text-match scores, word proximity and anchor text (the text of links that point to a page).

traffic estimation. Pages with heavy traffic but low PageRank are pages that people visit but do not link to.
crawl order. On the Stanford web, PageRank computed on a partial crawl predicts a page’s final backlink count better than the backlink count seen so far. Backlink counting stays inside the local cluster it started in, while PageRank finds the Stanford home page early and moves out from it.

An 80/20 share means the top 20\% of observations, sorted by value, contribute 80\% of the total. For income, the observations are people and the value is income. Calling them “causes” and “outcomes” adds a causal claim that the ratio cannot establish.

Definition 1. 

A Type-I Pareto random variable X has minimum value x_m>0 and shape parameter \alpha>0. Its survival function gives the probability of exceeding a threshold:
\overline F(x)=\Pr(X>x)=
\begin{cases}
\left(\dfrac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha, & x\ge x_m,\\[0.5em]
1, & x<x_m.
\end{cases}

Above the minimum, doubling a threshold multiplies the fraction exceeding it by 2^{-\alpha}. Smaller \alpha therefore means a heavier tail: more probability remains at large values. Taking the negative derivative of the survival function gives the density:
f(x)=\frac{\alpha x_m^\alpha}{x^{\alpha+1}},\qquad x\ge x_m.
top shares
Assume \alpha>1, so the mean is finite:
\mathbb E[X]=\int_{x_m}^{\infty}xf(x)\,dx
=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1}.
Let p be the fraction of observations in the upper group, with 0<p\le1. Its cutoff x_p satisfies \Pr(X>x_p)=p, giving x_p=x_m p^{-1/\alpha}. Integrating xf(x) above that cutoff gives the upper group’s share of expected value:
S(p)=\frac{\int_{x_p}^{\infty}xf(x)\,dx}{\mathbb E[X]}
=\left(\frac{x_m}{x_p}\right)^{\alpha-1}
=p^{1-1/\alpha}.
For the 80/20 split,
\left(\frac15\right)^{1-1/\alpha}=\frac45
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha=\frac{\ln5}{\ln4}\approx1.161.
This identifies one member of the Pareto family. Other distributions can have the same 80/20 share; that single ratio cannot identify the full distribution. For 0<\alpha\le1, the mean diverges and this population-share calculation loses its finite denominator. A finite sample still has a total, with shares that vary between samples.

A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off while making nobody worse off. An allocation is Pareto-efficient when no feasible Pareto improvement exists. Both judgments depend on which alternatives are feasible and whose preferences count. Stanford’s game-theory examples show how several allocations can satisfy this condition.

zero-sum game 

In a zero-sum game, every feasible outcome is Pareto-efficient with respect to the modeled payoffs: increasing one player’s payoff requires decreasing someone else’s. The same argument holds when the sum is any fixed constant. This says nothing about whether an outcome is a Nash equilibrium. See constant-sum games and Pareto optimality.

a measure of uncertainty in the value of a sample from a discrete probability distribution.

The larger the perplexity, the less likely it is that an observer can guess the value which will be drawn from the distribution.

probability distribution
The perplexity PP of a discrete probability distribution p is defined as:
PP(p) = \prod_{x} p(x)^{-p(x)} = b^{-\sum_{x} p(x) \log_b p(x)}
where x ranges over the events, 0^{-0} is defined to be 1, and b can be 2, 10, e, or any positive value other than 1.
The logarithm \log PP(p) is the entropy of the distribution; it is expressed in bits if b = 2, and in nats if the natural logarithm is used.
For a uniform distribution over exactly k outcomes (each with probability 1/k), the perplexity is simply k. This models a fair k-sided die, where perplexity k indicates uncertainty equivalent to rolling such a die.

Important 

perplexity is the exponentiation of entropy.


Entropy measures the expected number of bits required to encode the outcome using an optimal variable-length code.
probability model
Given a probability model q and test sample x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N drawn from unknown distribution p, the perplexity of model q is:
b^{-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \log_b q(x_i)} = \left(\prod_i q(x_i)\right)^{-1/N}
where b is customarily 2. Better models assign higher probabilities q(x_i) to test events, yielding lower perplexity.
The exponent -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \log_b q(x_i) represents cross entropy:
H(\tilde{p}, q) = -\sum_x \tilde{p}(x) \log_b q(x)
where \tilde{p} denotes the empirical distribution of the test sample (\tilde{p}(x) = n/N if x appeared n times in the test sample of size N).
By KL divergence definition: H(\tilde{p}, q) = H(\tilde{p}) + D_{KL}(\tilde{p} \| q) \geq H(\tilde{p}).

perplexity is minimized when q = \tilde{p}.

perplexity per token
In natural language processing, perplexity per token is defined as:
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} q(s_i)\right)^{-1/N}
where s_1, \ldots, s_n are the n documents in the corpus and N is the total number of tokens. This normalizes perplexity by text length, enabling meaningful comparisons.
For language models, perplexity per token can be computed as:
PPL(D) = \sqrt[N]{\frac{1}{m(T)}} = 2^{-\frac{1}{N}\log_2(m(T))}
where N is the number of tokens in test set T. This equals exponentiated cross-entropy, where cross-entropy H(p; m) is approximated as:
H(p; m) = -\frac{1}{N}\log_2(m(T))
as a language-model metric
Perplexity per token is the standard intrinsic metric for autoregressive language models that assign a probability to the next token (GPT-style). It does not apply cleanly to masked models like BERT, whose objective is not a left-to-right likelihood.
Lower perplexity does not guarantee better downstream performance: it correlates weakly with task metrics such as word error rate in speech recognition.
brown corpus
The lowest published perplexity on the Brown Corpus (1 million words of American English) as of 1992 was about 247 per token, corresponding to cross-entropy of \log_2 247 = 7.95 bits per word or 1.75 bits per letter using a trigram model.
Simply guessing “the” achieves 7% accuracy, contrasting with the 1/247 = 0.4\% expected from naive perplexity interpretation. This underscores the importance of the statistical model used and perplexity’s nuanced nature as a predictiveness measure.

He is the hard one, but I respect rigorous discipline. It was known that the people in Königsberg often formed a routine surrounding his mode of living.1
Kant is also known to be rather paradigmatic with his whole ethical framework of reasons. In a way, we are living in a Kantian world, where there is a universal concept of reason that transcends all linguistic and cultural boundaries.
The framework works like this. A moral rule binds me because reason gives it, so it binds every rational agent in the same way, whatever they happen to want. The test is the categorical imperative: act only on a maxim that you could also will as a universal law.2 Consequences and feelings do not settle the question. See ethics for the three formulations and the standard objections.
In a way, Kant IS emblematic of this certain notion of philosophy.
ontology framework.
see also: Critique of Pure Reason
The first Critique (1781, revised 1787) starts from a question about knowledge. Some judgments add content and still hold necessarily, such as 7+5=12 or “every event has a cause”. Experience alone cannot show necessity, so Kant asks how these synthetic a priori judgments are possible.
His answer is transcendental idealism. Space and time are the forms in which anything appears to us, and the categories of the understanding, such as cause and substance, are the rules by which we combine appearances into objects. Those structures come from the knowing subject, which is why they hold for every possible experience. The price is a limit: we know things as they appear, and we cannot know things as they are in themselves. Readers still dispute whether “thing in itself” names a second set of objects or the same objects considered apart from how they appear to us.3

Apology
Plato presents Socrates’ defence at his trial in Athens in 399 BCE. This is a composed account of the speech, so Socrates here means Plato’s Socrates.
Two sets of accusations matter (Apology 18a–24b):

The old public image: a natural philosopher who studies the sky and the earth, makes weak arguments defeat strong ones, and charges for teaching. Socrates denies that this describes his activity.
The formal indictment: corrupting the young and failing to acknowledge the city’s gods while introducing new divine beings.

Socrates says that anyone can listen to him, rich or poor, without paying. He denies having a body of instruction that makes him responsible for everything a listener later does (33a–b).
The oracle at Delphi said that nobody was wiser than Socrates. He tests this by questioning people reputed to be wise (20e–23b):

Politicians appear knowledgeable until they have to give an account of what they claim to know.
Poets produce fine work, yet cannot adequately explain it. Socrates attributes their success to inspiration and questions the further wisdom they claim on its strength.
Craftsmen really do know things he does not. Their mistake is treating expertise in a craft as authority about the most important human questions.

His advantage is limited: where he lacks knowledge, he does not suppose that he possesses it. The oracle gives him a reason to keep examining people. It also explains the resentment: an audience may enjoy someone’s embarrassment while the person being questioned blames Socrates.
Does the examination need to embarrass people? What makes wisdom so good?
Dialog
The dikasts are the citizen jurors. Socrates argues that Meletus has not thought through the charge of corrupting the young. Meletus first treats practically everyone except Socrates as an improving influence; Socrates challenges this using the example of the few people capable of training horses. He then argues that deliberate corruption would expose him to harm from those around him (24c–26a).
Socrates says that he would continue philosophising even if acquittal required him to stop. His divine obligation takes priority over that demand (29c–30b). He also refuses to obtain acquittal by bringing his children before the jury to solicit pity: the jury should decide according to justice and its oath (34b–35d).
The doctor prosecuted by a pastry-cook before children belongs to Gorgias 521e–522a. It describes the political vulnerability of someone who improves people through unpleasant treatment. It is not a quotation from the Apology.
Context of the trial
The trial follows Athens’ defeat in the Peloponnesian War and the rule of the Thirty. Socrates’ associations with Alcibiades and Critias form part of that political background. Calling him a scapegoat does not, by itself, establish why the jurors convicted him.
His own defence includes resistance to two regimes. Under the democracy, he opposed an illegal collective trial of generals; under the Thirty, he refused an order to help arrest Leon for execution (Apology 32a–e). His stated rule is to avoid injustice even when an authority demands it.
Reaction: Convicted by the stupidity of them all.
The wider proposal that philosophers should rule belongs to the Republic (473c–e). It requires education and knowledge of the good; inherited rank does not supply that knowledge. Keep this proposal separate from the defence speech and its particular jury.
Nietzsche questions Socrates’ commitment to reason. The unexamined life is not worth living (Apology 38a): what makes examination worth this much?

Socratic Idea of Good
The recurring demand is care for the soul: examine whether one’s judgments and actions are just, instead of letting money, reputation or power decide what matters (Apology 29d–30b).
What does wisdom do for us? In Euthydemus 278e–282d, possessions and abilities benefit us through their right use. Wisdom directs that use. Merely having more resources does not settle whether they make a life go well.
What is not good might not be wise?
If Socrates really cares about Athens, why does he avoid its public debates? He says his divine sign, the daimonion, turns him away from proposed actions and has kept him from a political career. Someone consistently resisting public injustice would soon be killed (31c–32a). His examples of resisting both regimes also limit the claim that he never participated in public affairs.
At the trial the sign is silent, including during his defence. Socrates takes this as a reason to hope that the outcome is good (40a–c). His refusal to escape is argued separately in Crito 46b–54d, through the question of whether escape would be just.
He knows there is a life after death? The Apology leaves two possibilities: dreamless unconsciousness or a migration of the soul (40c–41c). His claim that a good person cannot be harmed (41c–d) therefore needs its ethical sense kept in view: execution cannot force him to commit injustice. The trial plainly can kill him.
Doing wrong is worse than suffering wrong is defended in Gorgias 469b–c. The further claim that wrongdoing comes from ignorance concerns what an agent takes to be good; knowing a rule is not yet the wisdom Socrates seeks. These claims need arguments of their own.

Phaedo
Socrates spends his last day discussing the soul with friends in prison. The sacred mission to Delos has delayed his execution (Phaedo 58a–c). In prison he has composed a hymn to Apollo and put Aesop’s fables into verse, responding to a recurring dream that told him to practise music (60d–61b).
Death is the separation of soul and body. Philosophical training prepares for it by disciplining bodily desires and reasoning about things such as equality or justice themselves (64c–67e). This account depends on the soul being capable of thought apart from the body. Calling the body a distraction does not establish that independence.
Is there another side? Life after death? The arguments seem contrived and unconvincing; identify the premise being asked for each time.

Opposites (70c–72e). Waking comes from sleeping, and sleeping from waking. Socrates extends this pattern to life and death: the living must also come from the dead. The disputed step is whether that cycle applies to death and requires surviving souls.
Recollection (72e–77a). Equal-looking sticks can fall short of Equality itself. Socrates argues that judging the shortfall requires prior acquaintance with Equality, acquired before birth. This assumes that sensory learning cannot explain the standard. Pre-existence would still leave survival after death to be shown.
Affinity (78b–80b). Bodies resemble visible, changing, composite things; souls resemble intelligible and stable things. Socrates infers that a soul is less liable to dissolution. Resemblance to an indissoluble thing does not yet prove that a soul is indissoluble. Simmias’ harmony and Cebes’ weaver objections press the possibility that a soul could still perish (85e–88b).
Life-bearing soul (102a–107b). What necessarily brings a property excludes its opposite: three brings oddness, fire brings heat, and soul brings life. Socrates argues that soul therefore excludes death. To establish survival he also needs the deathless to be indestructible, a further premise explicitly accepted in the dialogue. The argument depends on these Forms and their relation to souls, not merely on the definition of a living body.

Phaedo, full text, especially 105c–107b for the final distinction between excluding death and surviving destruction.
Socrates drinks the poison calmly. His final instruction to Crito concerns a cock owed to Asclepius (118a), the healing god. Reading this as gratitude for release from bodily life is an interpretation; the line does not state which illness has been cured. The dialogue ends with Phaedo’s praise of his friend, rather than an independent confirmation of the afterlife.
Symposium
The banquet at Agathon’s house takes place while Socrates is alive. A later narrator recounts it from another participant’s report (Symposium 172a–173b).
Alcibiades describes the conflict Socrates produces in him: he is ashamed of neglecting his soul, then returns to the public approval he wants (215a–216c). His attempted seduction treats his beauty as something to exchange for Socrates’ wisdom. Socrates questions both the exchange and Alcibiades’ estimate of what he would receive (217a–219d). Alcibiades’ frustration does not establish that Socrates regards him as incapable of learning.
Socratic irony needs attention to the particular exchange. In Euthyphro 4e–5a, Socrates invites the man confidently prosecuting his own father to teach him what piety is. The invitation exposes Euthyphro’s claim to knowledge to questioning. Calling everything Socrates says insincere would erase the inquiry along with the mockery.
Love must be more than intense alliances with others. Diotima’s account moves from attachment to one beautiful body toward beautiful souls, practices, knowledge and Beauty itself (Symposium 210a–212a). Alcibiades’ speech brings that account back to a particular attachment that remains unresolved. Symposium, full text.
Republic
Metaphysics asks what there is and what it is. Plato’s Forms are intelligible objects, such as Beauty itself, distinguished from the many beautiful things we perceive (Republic 475e–480a). A sensible thing may appear beautiful in one respect and ugly in another; the Form supplies the stable object of inquiry.

Republic
Metaphysics asks what there is and what it is. Plato’s Forms are intelligible objects, such as Beauty itself, distinguished from the many beautiful things we perceive (Republic 475e–480a). A sensible thing may appear beautiful in one respect and ugly in another; the Form supplies the stable object of inquiry.
Socrates makes knowledge of the Good necessary for the education of the rulers (504d–506b). Everyone pursues what they take to be good, so mistaken judgments about the good can misdirect a whole life or city. His claim still leaves the problem of explaining what the Good is. He offers the sun analogy because he is not giving a direct account of it (506d–e).
Satisfied with opinion where knowledge is out there to be found?
Doxa is opinion; epistēmē is knowledge. Their distinction concerns their objects and the understanding one can give of them. A belief can happen to be true while its holder lacks an account of why it is true. The Republic’s divided line develops a more specific hierarchy of cognitive states (509d–511e).
Sun: Visible Things : Sight
The analogy has two corresponding relations (Republic 507b–509c):

The sun makes visible things visible and enables the eye to see them.
The Good makes intelligible things knowable and enables the mind to know them.

Socrates extends the relation: the sun sustains growth, and the Good gives the objects of knowledge their being and essence. He places the Good beyond being in dignity and power (509b).
The divided line distinguishes four states (509d–511e):

Eikasia: apprehension of images, shadows and reflections.
Pistis: belief concerning the visible things those images depict.
Dianoia: reasoning from hypotheses, exemplified by mathematics.
Noēsis: dialectical understanding that examines those hypotheses and seeks a first principle.

The mathematical diagram is visible; the square being studied is intelligible. Mathematical reasoning remains hypothetical when it takes its starting points for granted. Perception alone therefore does not name every state below philosophical understanding.
Dialetic
Dialectic seeks an account of what each thing is and tests that account through objections. In Republic 532a–534c, it examines the hypotheses the mathematical disciplines leave standing and aims to reach an unhypothetical first principle. A person who claims knowledge of the Good must be able to defend an account of it.
How do we understand philosophy? Here the demand is to explain and defend one’s starting points as well as the conclusions drawn from them. Whether Plato’s proposed ascent reaches a secure first principle remains a question for the argument.

a sub-class of policy optimization methods. Unlike value-based methods (which learn a value function to derive a policy), policy optimization methods directly learn a policy function \pi that selects actions without consulting a value function.
For policy gradient to apply, the policy function is parameterized as a differentiable \pi_\theta with parameters \theta.
overview
In policy-based RL, the actor is a parameterized policy function \pi_\theta, where \theta are the parameters of the actor. The actor takes the state s and produces a probability distribution
\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)

Discrete actions:
\sum_a \pi_\theta(a\mid s)=1
Continuous actions:
\int_a \pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,\mathrm da=1

The goal of policy optimization is to find \theta that maximizes the expected episodic reward J(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}\left[\sum_{t\in 0:T}\gamma^t R_t\;\Big|\;S_0=s_0\right]
where:

\gamma is the discount factor,
R_t is the reward at step t,
s_0 is the starting state,
T is the time horizon (possibly infinite).

The policy gradient is \nabla_\theta J(\theta)
Different policy gradient methods stochastically estimate \nabla_\theta J(\theta) in different ways.
The goal is to iteratively maximize J(\theta) by gradient ascent; since the key part is stochastic estimation, these are also studied under “Monte Carlo gradient estimation”.
